did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with the phrase “Praise the LORD” and with a person addressing his own soul: “Praise the LORD, my soul.” In this way, praise is presented as both a personal and an inward act.
The psalmist pledges to praise the LORD “while I live” and sing praises to him “as long as I exist”—that is, for as long as he lives. Praise is therefore connected to the length of a person’s life.
The chapter warns against trusting in “princes”—those in positions of power or other important people—because even human beings cannot provide complete salvation.
The verse describes human frailty: a person’s spirit departs, he returns to the ground, and on that very day “his plans perish”—his thoughts and plans cease to exist.
The expression “the God of Jacob” recalls the LORD’s special relationship with the people of Israel, and the verse presents the happy person as one whose hope rests in the LORD.
The LORD is described as the Creator of “heaven and earth” as well as “the sea and everything in them.” Alongside his creative power, the verse emphasizes his faithfulness “forever.”

Beginning with this verse, the chapter lists acts of kindness and justice: the LORD upholds the cause of the oppressed, gives food to the hungry, and sets prisoners free. The description of the LORD therefore also focuses on his care for people in distress.
In this verse, the name “the LORD” appears three times, and each time a different action is described: giving sight to the blind, lifting up those who are bowed down, and loving the righteous.
The chapter names three groups in need of protection—foreigners, orphans, and widows—and contrasts them with the way of the wicked, which the LORD “frustrates.”

“Praise the LORD” appears both at the beginning and at the end of the chapter, creating a literary frame for the hymn. The conclusion emphasizes that the LORD’s reign continues “forever” and “from generation to generation.”
